appraisal_events.evidence: il fallait adhérer tacitement à un Credo... l'orthodoxie de la petite église... elle avait l'habitude de prendre au propre les expressions figurées des émotions qu'elle éprouvait... « Qui sait, cela lui fera peut-être beaucoup plus de bien que vous n'alliez pas le déranger ce soir »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator ironically exposes Mme Verdurin's salon as a quasi-religious cult of exclusion built on absurdly inflated claims about her proteges, her comic literal-mindedness about her own emotions, and her manipulative persuasion of Cottard to neglect a dying patient for her own comfort.

appraisal_events.evidence: une personne presque du demi-monde, Mme de Crécy... personnes ignorantes du monde et à la naïveté de qui il avait été si facile de faire accroire que la princesse de Sagan et la duchesse de Guermantes étaient obligées de payer des malheureux pour avoir du monde à leurs dîners... l'ancienne concierge et la cocotte eussent dédaigneusement refusé
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator ironically portrays Odette, alongside the pianist's aunt, as socially naive and easily deceived by Verdurin propaganda, imagining herself too grand to accept invitations to the truly fashionable houses she does not understand.

status_effects.explanation: Mme Verdurin is portrayed throughout the passage as absurdly self-important, controlling, and given to comic excess, undercutting any claim to genuine discernment or authority.
Odette's standing is locally diminished by the narrator's portrait of her as a naive, easily flattered demi-mondaine unaware of real social hierarchies.

ambiguities: The naiveté described is shared jointly with the pianist's aunt, an unnamed figure not on the reference sheet, so the diminishment targets Odette as the named representative of a portrayal that is not exclusively about her alone.
